newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S. African truth commission gets tough.
newsitem.headline: S. African truth commission gets tough.

text.p: South Africa's official probe into the human rights history of apartheid is switching the emphasis of its work from the reconciliation offered by hundreds of blacks to the truth being hidden by scores of whites.

Archbishop Desmond Tutu's state-financed Truth and Reconciliation Commission (TRC) has so far heard mainly from black victims of apartheid, most of whom offered forgiveness in return for information about the fate of their loved ones.
The soldiers, policemen and politicians who could reveal the truth about the campaign against black liberation, the death squads and torture have largely stayed away.
President Nelson Mandela's vision of a healing blend of disclosure, forgiveness and compensation is failing to emerge.
In Upington last week, a junior official confirmed a persistent rumour when he told a commission hearing that police there had shredded a pile of files "as big as a table".

Deputy TRC chairman Alex Boraine said in an interview that many key files probably had been destroyed since the April 1994 election that ousted F. W. de Klerk's white-led government in favour of Mandela's black-led one.
Frustration with the white reluctance to admit the truth of the fight against black empowerment led Tutu to warn last week that inside the TRC's velvet glove was a fist of steel.

At the end of the week Boraine announced that former Law and Order Minister Adriaan Vlok and eight retired police chiefs and generals would be the first apartheid managers to be hauled before the commission by subpoena.

"We have said we will use the carrot, but there is also a stick. There are the powers laid down in the (National Unity and Reconciliation) Act which we can use when we want to use them. We have decided that time has come," he said.

The TRC's offer of amnesty in return for a full and voluntary confession of politically motivated human rights crimes, which expires on December 16, has lured only a handful of former agents of apartheid.

"The commission is not and doesn't want to be seen as a witchhunt. We didn't want to start at the extreme end, but we have made it very clear that we will not hesitiate to use our powers when it becomes necessary.
"In our view that time has arrived," Boraine said.

So far, courts prosecuting former agents of the apartheid state, including self-confessed multiple killer Eugene de Kock, known to his colleagues as "Prime Evil", have uncovered far more detail about apartheid's crimes than the commission.
Boraine said that was about to change.
The commission last week received its first amnesty applications from policemen not facing immediate prosecution for human rights crimes committed in defence of apartheid.
Though he declined to give details, Boraine said preliminary evidence by the five unidentified policemen had answered many of the mysteries of the apartheid era killings and disappearances.
Boraine said it was not surprising that apartheid's criminals were waiting until the last moment to seek amnesty, waiting to see whether they would be implicated and face trial.
